indicators.note: Something done loudly is done aloud rather than on paper, so the wordplay hands you a sound and leaves the spelling to you.

parts.note: what rips at the furniture claws at it, and CLAWS said out loud is written down quite differently

explanation.surface: Someone noisily tearing up a page of a contract.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rips' looks like a verb belonging to the surface story of destroyed paperwork, and the sound you need out of it belongs to a cat.
explanation.definitionFit: A clause is one numbered provision of a contract, the unit lawyers point at when they argue over what was actually agreed.

clue.text: Vacant colonel with temper makes stupid mistake

indicators.note: A vacant building has had everything between its walls removed, so the word keeps only the letters at its two ends.

parts.note: COLONEL emptied of everything inside it leaves the C and the L standing at its ends
to be in a temper is to be in an anger — the two nouns swap freely

explanation.surface: An empty-headed colonel losing his temper and getting something badly wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vacant' reads as a description of the colonel — dim, absent-minded — while it is quietly an instruction to hollow the word out.
explanation.definitionFit: A clanger is a blunder loud enough that everyone in the room notices — you drop one, the way a bell rings out in a silence.

parts.note: to aver something is to state it flatly, the way a witness does

indicators.note: What happens initially happens at the very start, so only the opening letter of the word standing beside it is taken.

parts.note: the opening letter of Tracing

explanation.surface: Dodging the government's surveillance right at the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' is the trap: it reads as the government doing the tracing, and it is the verb aver, to declare something as fact.
explanation.definitionFit: To avert something is to turn it aside before it arrives — you avert your eyes, or avert a disaster — which is deflecting it.

clue.text: Coy about question by a school's head being soft

indicators.note: To be about something is to be all round it, so this word wraps itself over the pieces named after it.

parts.note: coy and shy both describe someone hanging back from attention
qu. is the standard short form of question, on a form or in a textbook

indicators.note: The head of anything is its front end, so only the leading letter of the word it belongs to is used.

parts.note: the article is lifted straight out of the clue as a single letter
the front letter of School

explanation.surface: A shy pupil ducking a question put to them by the head of a school.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'school's head' sounds like a person and asks for one letter, and 'question' contracts to the two-letter qu. rather than the single Q you would expect.
explanation.definitionFit: Something squashy gives way the moment you press it — an overripe peach, a beanbag — which is soft in the yielding sense.

parts.note: PA is the everyday short form of personal assistant
to exploit a resource is to use it

explanation.surface: A personal assistant turning every interruption to their own advantage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exploits' can be a noun meaning daring deeds, which is how the surface would like to be read; the wordplay wants the plain verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A pause is a short break in something already running — speech, music, a meeting — so pauses are the interruptions of it.

clue.text: Charm a stubborn person over time

indicators.note: This entry runs downwards, and one thing over another sits above it, so the pieces named first are stacked on top of the last.

parts.note: the article taken as it stands from the clue
a mule is proverbially obstinate, and the word is used of people who will not budge
t is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Slowly winning over an obstinate person as the years go by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charm' is the noun for a lucky object, not the verb for winning someone round, and the surface leans its whole weight on the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An amulet is an object worn to keep harm off, so it is a charm in the lucky-token sense rather than the personal-appeal one.

clue.text: Spend a lot of money, getting belt aboard jet

indicators.note: Anything taken aboard is carried within the vessel, so one piece travels inside the other rather than beside it.

parts.note: a jet of water is a spout of it
to belt someone is to lash them — both are blows, not straps

explanation.surface: A big spender taking a belt on board a private jet.
explanation.walkthrough: Both short words are doing violence to your expectations: a belt is a blow rather than something worn, and a jet is a spurt of water rather than an aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: To splash out is the British idiom for spending freely on something you did not strictly need — opening the wallet wide.

indicators.note: The plainest container word there is — what is in something sits inside it, here between the letters of the piece named next.

parts.note: the sum of a thing is the whole of it, as in 'the sum total'
a tern is a small sea bird, and one of the crossword's regulars

explanation.surface: A bird studied whole, bones and all.
explanation.walkthrough: TERN is worth banking as vocabulary, and 'in entirety' reads as a single phrase while the clue needs it as two separate words.
explanation.definitionFit: The sternum is the breastbone, the flat plate running down the front of the ribcage where the ribs meet.

clue.text: Offer card to editor being kind

parts.note: you tender a resignation, and a tender is a formal offer to do a job
one of the four suits in a pack of playing cards
ed is the usual short form of editor

explanation.surface: Handing a greetings card to your editor to show you care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Card' does the real hiding: it reads as something you buy in a shop and post, and the wordplay wants a red suit.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone tender-hearted is easily moved by other people's troubles, which is kind in the soft, sympathetic sense.

definitions.meaning: the verb: to add spirits to somebody's drink without telling them
the noun: fabric made of fine threads knotted into an open mesh

explanation.surface: An instruction to drive a spike through some netting.
explanation.walkthrough: Two senses sit side by side with nothing joining them: the verb for doctoring a drink, and the noun for openwork fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: To lace a drink is to spike it with alcohol, and lace is netting in the sense of a fine open fabric of knotted threads.

clue.text: A dull queen strangely without peer

indicators.note: Something done strangely is not done the usual way, so the letters beside it refuse to stay in the order they arrived in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A tedious monarch behaving oddly and with no equal anywhere in the land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without peer' looks like part of the picture of a lonely queen with no equals at court, and peer there means an equal, which makes it the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Unequalled says nothing matches it, and 'without peer' makes the same claim using the older sense of peer, an equal.

parts.note: the article gives up its shorter form, a single letter
a gate is the entrance through a wall or a fence
S is the size abbreviation for small, as on any clothing label

explanation.surface: A doorway set about with little stones.
explanation.walkthrough: The sentence reads as one continuous description of a gateway, so the join between wordplay and definition falls inside the picture rather than at a natural pause.
explanation.definitionFit: Agates are banded semi-precious stones, the striped ones cut for cheap jewellery and rolled as marbles.

indicators.note: To redesign something is to build it again to a different plan out of the same materials, so these letters end up in a new arrangement.

parts.note: d is the standard abbreviation for director
anagram fodder, seven letters once the apostrophe is dropped

explanation.surface: A film director giving the singer's stage outfit a makeover.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'singer's' reads as an ordinary possessive, and its S is one of the eight letters being shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Dressing and clothing are both the verbal noun for putting garments on somebody — what you are doing while you get dressed.

parts.note: a grave expression is a serious one; this adjective has nothing to do with burial
a yard is three feet, a unit of distance

explanation.surface: A long hard trek still to go before anywhere you could stop and rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Serious' means grave in the sense of a solemn face, an adjective that arrived in English by a completely separate route from the burial noun it happens to spell.
explanation.definitionFit: A graveyard is the ground where the dead are laid to rest, and 'resting place' is the standard euphemism for exactly that.

indicators.note: What has been developed has been worked up into a shape quite unlike the material it started from, so the letters do not stay put.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters once the apostrophe is dropped

explanation.surface: A performer boasting about the air of talent they have developed over the years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air' is a verb here, not the noun the surface offers, and it is doing the defining from the very first word of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To ventilate a room is to air it, letting fresh air move through, and both verbs also cover airing a grievance in public.

definitions.meaning: the school sense: a year group of pupils taught together in Britain
the etiquette sense: the accepted way of behaving, praised or condemned as good or bad

explanation.surface: The etiquette that governs a school classroom.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a school year group is a form, and behaving as expected is good form — two senses that share nothing but their spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A form is a class in a British school — the third form, the sixth form — and form is also the done thing, as in 'good form'.

clue.text: Smooth leaders of society attracting new devotees

indicators.note: A leader walks at the front of the group, so the front letter of each word that follows is what you collect.

parts.note: the opening letter of Society
the opening letter of Attracting
the opening letter of New
the opening letter of Devotees

explanation.surface: Prominent members of society picking up a fresh crop of followers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smooth' sits where an adjective describing those leaders would sit, and it is the verb — what you do to a rough plank.
explanation.definitionFit: To sand a surface is to rub it down with abrasive paper until it is smooth, so the verb takes its name from the grit.

indicators.note: Putting one thing into another leaves it enclosed, so the piece named first is buried inside the piece named last.

parts.note: an upswing in prices is a surge in them
Co. is the abbreviation printed on any firm's letterhead

explanation.surface: Driving a struggling firm hard until its fortunes turn upward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whip' reads as the verb for driving somebody on, and the definition wants the noun — the object doing the driving.
explanation.definitionFit: A scourge is a whip of knotted cords, the flogging kind, long before the word came to mean any affliction.

indicators.note: To cavort is to caper about with no order to it at all, so the letters beside this word will not stand still.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: A family of limber relations larking about together.
explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration is the whole hint on a three-word clue: only one of the three words is nine letters long, which settles which is fodder and which is definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone versatile turns their hand to anything, which is flexible in the adaptable sense rather than the physically bendy one.

clue.text: Division of, say, soldiers in street

indicators.note: Whatever is in something sits inside it, so the pieces named before this word drop between the letters of the one after it.

parts.note: St is the abbreviation on any road sign
eg introduces an example, which is the job 'say' does in a sentence
the men of a regiment are its soldiers, as in 'officers and men'

explanation.surface: A division of soldiers drawn up in the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Division of, say, soldiers' invites you to read the whole opening as one definition; only the first word is, and 'say' is the abbreviation eg.
explanation.definitionFit: A segment is a piece cut off a whole — an orange segment, a segment of a circle — so it is a division of that thing.

indicators.note: Rearranging furniture keeps every piece and changes only where each one stands, which is what happens to these letters.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: A gallery that has had most of its pictures rehung.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mostly' looks like an instruction to take most of a word and drop the rest, which is its usual job in a clue; here it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Largely and mostly both mean for the greater part: a statement largely true is true across most of it.

clue.text: Aromatic plant found in swamp and North Eastern lake

parts.note: a fen is low waterlogged ground; the Fens of eastern England are the best known stretch
NE is the compass abbreviation for north eastern
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A herb growing wild by a marsh beside a lake in the north east.
explanation.walkthrough: Everything after the definition is landscape vocabulary, which is why the sentence reads as a line from a field guide rather than as three instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: Fennel is a feathery herb with a strong aniseed smell, grown for its seeds and its bulb, so it is an aromatic plant.

indicators.note: Someone carrying a package has it on their person, inside their coat, so this word takes the next piece within itself.

parts.note: a doer is someone who acts rather than talks — 'a doer, not a dreamer'
a mine is an explosive charge, buried or moored, waiting to be set off

explanation.surface: A go-getter walking around with a bomb on them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Explosive' reads as an adjective describing that energetic person, and the wordplay needs the noun — a specific device.
explanation.definitionFit: To domineer over people is to bully them into doing as you say, which is what browbeating them amounts to.

indicators.note: A bit of something is a piece broken out of the middle of it, so a run of letters is lifted from inside the words that follow.

parts.note: six consecutive letters run from the tail of the first word straight into the second

explanation.surface: A factory keeping its production line running through the night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bit of' is about as quiet as a hidden-word signal gets, because it reads as a scrap of the manufacturing, which is exactly what the surface needs it to mean.
explanation.definitionFit: To govern is to control — a country, a company, or the speed of an engine, which is where a governor takes its name from.

indicators.note: What comes after something follows behind it, so the piece named first in the clue is written second in the answer.

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals
the everyday vehicle on the drive

explanation.surface: A car turning up after six o'clock to collect the parish priest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Six' is a Roman numeral rather than the hour the surface offers, and the vehicle ends up second despite being named first.
explanation.definitionFit: A vicar is the priest in charge of a Church of England parish, a post women have held since 1994, so the word covers either.

clue.text: Relative is unusually energetic around middle of day

indicators.note: What is done unusually is not done the usual way, so these letters abandon the order the clue lists them in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

indicators.note: Going around something means closing over it, so the letter named next is gathered in with the rest rather than left outside.

parts.note: the central letter of dAy

explanation.surface: A lively family member charging about the house at lunchtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Middle of day' reads as noon and asks instead for the letter standing between the D and the Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Your great-niece is the daughter of your niece or nephew, one further generation down the family tree, so she is a relative by blood.

clue.text: Cook cooked halved elephant fish heads

indicators.note: The head of a word is its first letter, and the plural asks for one from each of the words listed before it.

parts.note: the opening letter of Cooked
the opening letter of Halved
the opening letter of Elephant
the opening letter of Fish

explanation.surface: A recipe calling for half an elephant and a few fish heads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooked' and 'halved' both look like instructions to do something to their neighbours, and both are only there to donate a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A chef is a professional cook, the one running a kitchen rather than anybody who happens to be at the stove.

indicators.note: To hold something is to have it contained within your grasp, so the letters sit unbroken inside the words before this.
This entry runs across the grid, so back means reading from the right-hand end towards the left.

parts.note: six consecutive letters run from inside the first word straight into the second

explanation.surface: Beryl, who never manages to hold anything back for long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holds back' reads as one phrase meaning restrains, and the clue needs it as two words doing two different jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something evenly is to do it at a steady unvarying rate from start to finish, which is doing it consistently.

clue.text: Solid investigation involving leader of research

indicators.note: To involve someone is to draw them into the thing, so the letter named next ends up inside the word before it.

parts.note: a study of a problem is an investigation into it

indicators.note: A leader stands at the head of the line, so only the opening letter of the word that follows is taken.

parts.note: the first letter of Research

explanation.surface: A solid inquiry that brings the head of the research team on board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader of research' reads as a person running a project, and it asks for a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sturdy takes weight and knocks without giving, which is solid in the well-built sense rather than the not-hollow one.
